messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 40

At fifty-one, Layla manages a twelve-story hotel in the city center, but the building that houses her trauma is not on any official blueprint. Ten months ago, during the slow spring season, she descended into the sub-basement to review a vendor’s industrial fogging contract. The ventilation grates were offline for routine cleaning when a pressure valve on a tank of concentrated quaternary ammonium compound ruptured. The hiss of the escaping gas filled the concrete corridor. She held her breath, turned, and ran up the stairs, but the chemical cloud had already coated her throat and lungs. The medical evaluation cleared her physically, but her nervous system never accepted the all-clear. Now, the faintest whiff of ammonia triggers a sudden drop in her chest. Every morning, she stands in her executive office and watches the housekeeping carts roll down the hall. When the tang of citrus disinfectant drifts through the door, she steps back, locks the glass, and sits on the leather chair until her pulse steadies. She tells herself it is just lingering sensitivity. She has pulled the facility’s air quality reports three times this month. Managing the hotel used to mean walking every floor, greeting staff by name, troubleshooting a flooded suite at midnight. Now, she delegates the west wing to her assistant manager. She avoids the linen chutes, the boiler room, and the maintenance supply closet. During weekly staff meetings, she sits at the head of the table, but her hands rest on the polished wood, fingers tapping a quiet, uneven rhythm. When a guest mentions a “chemical smell” in their room, she feels a sudden, heavy drop in her stomach. She offers to relocate them immediately, even when no one has complained. At home, sleep has fractured. She wakes at two in the morning gasping, convinced the ventilation alarms are sounding. Her husband, Tariq, learns to move quietly when he comes in to check on her. She pulls the curtains shut during daylight hours, telling herself it helps her rest, but it is really to keep the world at a distance. She used to host large family gatherings, her mother’s Middle Eastern recipes—saffron rice, slow-braised lamb—filling the living room. Now, she eats before the kitchen odors accumulate. She catches herself flinching when the dishwasher cycles or the gas stove ignites. She replays the sub-basement moment on loops. Did she sign off on the equipment too quickly? Did she ignore the pressure gauge? Her mind builds labyrinths of what if. She feels detached from the colleagues who pat her shoulder, telling her to just breathe through it. Their voices sound muffled, like they are speaking from another room. She loves Tariq, but the emotional tether feels thin. She smiles when he asks about her day, but her words are careful, measured, stripped of the warmth that used to spill out naturally. It is Tuesday. A maintenance worker arrives with a canister of industrial solvent for the marble lobby. She watches him unscrew the cap from across the atrium. Her throat constricts. She walks to the side corridor, turns her face toward the service entrance, and breathes through her mouth until the clicking of his shoes fades. She checks her phone, reviews the weekly occupancy report, and calls Tariq to ask what time he wants dinner. Her voice is steady. The hotel hums around her, full of life and motion, but she moves through it like a person walking on thin ice, testing each step, listening for the crack.
